`SaveChanges` skips properties whose provider type differs from the CLR type unless `AutoDetectChangesEnabled` is set per property.

en.explanation: `DetectChanges` decides whether a property changed by comparing the snapshot with the current value using the property's `ValueComparer`. For a converted `List<string>` the default comparer uses `Equals`, i.e. reference equality, and the snapshot holds the same reference that was mutated in place, so nothing looks modified. Supply a `ValueComparer` that compares contents, computes a hash and creates a deep snapshot, or replace the converter with a primitive collection (EF Core 8+), which Npgsql maps to a `text[]` column with proper comparison. EF logs a warning for collection-typed properties with a converter but no comparer. Converters apply in both directions, and change tracking applies to converted properties like any other; `[ConcurrencyCheck]` and per-property `AutoDetectChangesEnabled` are unrelated or nonexistent.

options.text: Query filters are applied only to tracking queries; the orders endpoint uses `AsNoTracking()`.
`OnModelCreating` runs for every context instance, but filters are compiled once, so the closure is evaluated only for the first request.
Query filters cannot capture variables; EF silently drops a filter whose lambda references anything other than entity properties.

The model, including the filter, is built once per context type and cached; the local `tenantId` captured during that single run is frozen. The filter must reference a member of the context (e.g. a `TenantId` property), which EF evaluates per instance.

en.explanation: `OnModelCreating` executes once per context type per process; the resulting model is cached and reused by every instance. A local variable captured by the filter lambda becomes a constant value from whichever request built the model first, so every tenant gets that tenant's filter. EF special-cases member access on the context (`this.TenantId`) and turns it into a parameter evaluated per context instance. The `AsNoTracking` option is wrong: filters apply to every LINQ query of the entity type regardless of tracking. The "runs for every instance" option has the caching backwards. Filters can reference captured values; they are kept, which is precisely why the stale value is applied silently.

en.prompt: `Order` owns an `Address` via `OwnsOne(o => o.ShippingAddress)` with default configuration. Which statement is true?

options.text: The address is stored in the `Orders` table as prefixed columns (e.g. `ShippingAddress_City`), is loaded with the order without `Include`, and has no identity outside its owner.
The address gets its own `Addresses` table with a foreign key to `Orders`, and must be loaded with `Include(o => o.ShippingAddress)`.
The same `Address` instance can be assigned to the shipping address of two orders; EF stores a reference rather than copying values.
Owned types are only metadata for validation; EF ignores them unless they are also exposed as a `DbSet<Address>`.

en.explanation: `OwnsOne` defaults to table splitting: the owned type's properties become columns of the owner's table, prefixed with the navigation name, and EF always loads owned data together with the owner. The owned entity's key is a shadow copy of the owner's key, so it has no independent identity and cannot be queried through its own `DbSet`. A separate table is the default only for `OwnsMany` (or when you configure `ToTable` explicitly). Sharing one owned instance between two owners is not supported because each owned entity is tracked as part of exactly one owner; that is one reason EF Core 8 introduced complex types, which have true value semantics. Owned types are fully mapped and persisted; they must *not* have their own `DbSet`.

en.prompt: How would you map value objects (for example `Money` and `Address`) and strongly-typed ids (`OrderId`) in EF Core 10 with PostgreSQL? Compare owned types, complex types, value converters and JSON columns, and say when you would pick each.
en.explanation: Model answer: strongly-typed ids and single-value objects (`OrderId`, `Email`) map with value converters (`HasConversion`), optionally as a convention via `ConfigureConventions`; queries compare on the provider value, so methods of the CLR type are not translatable, and mutable types need a `ValueComparer`. Multi-property value objects (`Money` = amount + currency, `Address`) map as owned types (`OwnsOne`, columns in the owner's table, loaded with the owner, identity tied to the owner, not shareable) or, since EF Core 8, as complex types (`ComplexProperty`), which have no key, true value semantics and can be shared; EF Core 10 extends complex types (optional, JSON) and they are the better default for immutable value objects. `OwnsMany` uses a separate table. JSON columns (`ToJson()` on `jsonb`) suit aggregates or sparse/variable data read and written as a unit, with LINQ translated to JSON paths, but give up foreign keys, column-level constraints and simple indexing, so frequently filtered or joined data stays relational. Primitive collections map to PostgreSQL arrays.
rubric: Uses value converters (`HasConversion`) for strongly-typed ids or single-value objects, noting a limitation (translation on the provider value, or `ValueComparer` for mutable types).
Describes owned types (`OwnsOne` columns in the owner's table, loaded with the owner, no independent identity; `OwnsMany` separate table).
Mentions complex types (EF Core 8+) as value-semantics mapping without keys and contrasts them with owned types.
Describes JSON columns (`ToJson`/`jsonb`) with a sensible trade-off: good for documents or sparse data handled as a unit, poor for heavily filtered, joined or constrained data.

concepts.title: Bulk Operations and Performance: Compiled Queries, Batching, Bulk Libraries, When to Bypass EF

en.title: Bulk Operations and Performance: Compiled Queries, Batching, Bulk Libraries, When to Bypass EF
en.note:
## What it is

EF Core is fast enough for the vast majority of OLTP work if you avoid its traps; it is the wrong tool for moving millions of rows. Senior answers show both: how to make EF efficient, and where to stop using it.

## Where time goes in an EF query

1. **Query pipeline**: parameter extraction from the expression tree, cache lookup by expression shape, and, on a miss, translation to SQL. The **query cache** means a given LINQ shape is translated once per process, not per execution.
2. **Database**: plan and execution; the bulk of the time for real queries.
3. **Materialisation**: creating objects and, for tracking queries, snapshots and identity-map entries.

**Compiled queries** (`EF.CompileAsyncQuery((AppDbContext db, int id) => db.Orders.Single(o => o.Id == id))`) skip step 1's cache-key computation and parameter extraction. The gain is real but small, visible only on very hot, cheap queries; they do not change SQL or the database plan. **Compiled models** (`dotnet ef dbcontext optimize`) reduce startup time for very large models; EF Core 9+ can also precompile queries for NativeAOT (experimental).

**Query cache pollution** is the opposite problem: building expression trees dynamically with `Expression.Constant(value)` inlines each value into the SQL, so every distinct value is a new cache entry, a new translation and a new database plan. Capture values in closures (they become parameters), or use `EF.Parameter(...)`.

## Read path

- Project to DTOs with `Select`; fetch only needed columns; no tracking.
- `AsNoTracking` for read-only entity queries.
- Avoid N+1 and cartesian explosions (see loading strategies).
- Paginate (keyset over offset for deep pages) and stream with `AsAsyncEnumerable()` when processing large results instead of buffering with `ToListAsync()`.
- Context pooling (`AddDbContextPool`) for high request rates.

## Write path

- **Batching**: `SaveChanges` sends many statements in one round trip (Npgsql uses `NpgsqlBatch`; the batch size is configurable with `MaxBatchSize`). Batching reduces round trips, but it is still one statement per entity, and the entities must be loaded and tracked first.
- **Set-based updates/deletes**: `ExecuteUpdateAsync`/`ExecuteDeleteAsync` (EF Core 7+) issue a single statement without loading anything. They bypass the tracker, interceptors on `SaveChanges` and concurrency tokens.
- **Chunked processing**: for jobs that must use entities, process in chunks and `ChangeTracker.Clear()` (or use a new context) after each, or the growing tracker makes each `SaveChanges` slower.
- **Bulk inserts**: EF has no bulk insert. On PostgreSQL the fastest path is binary `COPY`: Npgsql's `BeginBinaryImportAsync`, or a library that uses it (`EFCore.BulkExtensions`, `linq2db.EntityFrameworkCore`'s `BulkCopy`, commercial Entity Framework Extensions). Check licences: `EFCore.BulkExtensions` moved to a dual licence that requires a paid licence for larger companies.

## When to bypass EF

- Bulk loads, ETL, migrations of data at scale: `COPY` or SQL scripts.
- Complex reporting queries with window functions, CTEs or vendor features: raw SQL via `SqlQuery<T>`/`FromSql`, or Dapper over the same `NpgsqlDataSource`.
- Hot paths where profiling proves EF overhead matters. Measure first; most slowness is the SQL, not EF.

## How to measure

- `LogTo`/`Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command` logs with elapsed times; `ToQueryString()`; OpenTelemetry instrumentation for Npgsql/EF.
- A `DbCommandInterceptor` that logs slow commands.
- `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the generated SQL; `pg_stat_statements` for the real workload.
- BenchmarkDotNet for micro-level claims (compiled vs regular queries).

```csharp
// 5 million rows: COPY, not SaveChanges. dataSource is the app's NpgsqlDataSource.
await using var conn = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
await using var importer = await conn.BeginBinaryImportAsync(
    "COPY readings (sensor_id, taken_at, value) FROM STDIN (FORMAT BINARY)", ct);
foreach (var r in readings)
{
    await importer.StartRowAsync(ct);
    await importer.WriteAsync(r.SensorId, NpgsqlDbType.Integer, ct);
    await importer.WriteAsync(r.TakenAt, NpgsqlDbType.TimestampTz, ct);
    await importer.WriteAsync(r.Value, NpgsqlDbType.Double, ct);
}
await importer.CompleteAsync(ct);
```

## Common misconceptions

- "EF re-translates LINQ every time; compiled queries fix that." The query cache already does; compiled queries shave the cache lookup.
- "`SaveChanges` batching is a bulk operation." It is still per-entity statements over loaded entities.
- "`AddRange` is a bulk insert." It is `Add` in a loop.
- "Dapper is always faster." For equivalent SQL with no tracking the difference is usually small.

en.prompt: You must set `Status = Archived` on 200,000 orders older than two years. Which approach is the most efficient with EF Core 10?

options.text: Load the orders, set `Status` on each and call `SaveChangesAsync()` once; EF batches the changes into a single `UPDATE` statement.
`await db.Orders.Where(o => o.CreatedAt < cutoff).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(o => o.Status, OrderStatus.Archived));`, a single set-based `UPDATE` without loading any entities.
Load the orders with `AsNoTracking()`, modify them and pass them to `UpdateRange`, which EF executes as a bulk update.
Wrap the load-modify-save version in `EF.CompileAsyncQuery` so the 200,000 updates are compiled once.

en.explanation: `ExecuteUpdateAsync` (EF Core 7+) translates the whole operation into one `UPDATE ... WHERE "CreatedAt" < @cutoff`: no rows travel to the client, nothing is tracked, one round trip. The trade-off is that it bypasses the change tracker, `SaveChanges` interceptors and concurrency tokens. The load-and-save option misunderstands batching: EF batches *statements* into fewer round trips, but it still sends 200,000 individual `UPDATE`s after materialising and tracking 200,000 entities. `UpdateRange` marks every property of every entity modified, which is even more data, not a bulk operation. Compiled queries apply to reads and only shave query-pipeline overhead; they do nothing for writes.

en.prompt: What does `EF.CompileAsyncQuery` actually save compared with running the same LINQ query normally?

options.text: Without it EF translates the LINQ expression to SQL on every execution; compiling translates it once, which typically halves query latency.
It turns the query into a server-side prepared statement, so PostgreSQL skips planning on subsequent executions.

It skips per-execution work in EF's query pipeline (computing the cache key from the expression tree and extracting parameters); SQL translation is already cached for normal queries, so the gain is small and matters only for very hot, cheap queries.
It is required for queries to be cached at all when they contain captured variables; otherwise each new variable value creates a new cache entry.

en.explanation: EF Core already caches translated queries by expression-tree shape; a normal execution still has to walk the expression tree to compute the cache key and extract parameter values, and that is the part a compiled query skips by holding a pre-built delegate. It does not change the SQL, the database plan, or materialisation, so benchmarks typically show a modest gain on trivial queries and noise on real ones. The "translates every time" option is the core misconception. Prepared statements are a separate concern handled by Npgsql (automatic preparation is configured via `Max Auto Prepare` in the connection string), not by compiled queries. Captured variables are parameterised and share one cache entry already; it is inlined *constants* that pollute the cache.

en.prompt: A job must load 5 million sensor readings from a file into a PostgreSQL table as fast as possible. Which approach fits?

options.text: Stream the rows through Npgsql's binary `COPY` (`BeginBinaryImportAsync`) or a bulk library built on it, bypassing the change tracker.
`AddRange` all 5 million entities and call `SaveChangesAsync()` once; EF turns it into one multi-row `INSERT`.
`Parallel.ForEachAsync` over the rows with a single shared `DbContext`, calling `Add` and `SaveChangesAsync` per row.
Call `ExecuteUpdateAsync` with an insert setter; EF Core 7+ supports set-based inserts through it.

en.explanation: PostgreSQL's `COPY ... FROM STDIN (FORMAT BINARY)` streams rows without per-statement parsing, planning or round trips and is typically an order of magnitude faster than batched `INSERT`s; Npgsql exposes it via `BeginBinaryImportAsync`, and libraries such as `linq2db.EntityFrameworkCore` or `EFCore.BulkExtensions` wrap it (check their licences). `AddRange` + `SaveChanges` tracks 5 million entities in memory and still sends individual `INSERT`s in batches; EF has no single bulk insert. Sharing one `DbContext` across parallel tasks throws ("a second operation was started"), and per-row saves maximise round trips. `ExecuteUpdate`/`ExecuteDelete` exist, but there is no `ExecuteInsert`; set-based inserts from a query need raw SQL (`INSERT ... SELECT`).

options.text: `Expression.Lambda` compiles a new delegate on every request, and those delegates are never collected.

`Expression.Constant` values are inlined into the SQL as literals, so every distinct `customerId` is a new query-cache entry, a new translation and a new statement for PostgreSQL to plan; build the tree so the value is a captured closure member (a parameter) or wrap it in `EF.Parameter`.
EF disables its query cache for manually built expression trees, so every request is translated from scratch regardless of the values.
Each request opens a new connection because dynamic queries cannot use Npgsql's pool, which causes the memory growth.

en.explanation: EF parameterises values that come from closures (member access on a captured object) and inlines `ConstantExpression`s as SQL literals. Because the cache key includes constants, each customer id yields a separate cache entry and translation (memory and CPU on the app side) and a distinct SQL text (plan-cache churn on the database side). Expressing the value as a member of a closure object, e.g. `Expression.Property(Expression.Constant(new { customerId }), "customerId")`, or using `EF.Parameter(customerId)` restores a single parameterised query. EF never calls `Compile()` on query expressions; it translates them. The cache is not disabled for hand-built trees; it simply keys them like any other. Connection pooling is independent of how the query was built.

en.prompt: An EF Core-based service has a slow read endpoint and a nightly batch job that takes hours. How do you find the bottlenecks and fix them, and at what point do you stop using EF Core for a given task?
en.explanation: Model answer: measure first: EF command logging with durations, `ToQueryString()`, OpenTelemetry spans or a slow-command interceptor, then `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and `pg_stat_statements` on the database side, and BenchmarkDotNet for micro-level claims. Read endpoint: check for N+1 and cartesian explosions, project to DTOs instead of loading entities, use `AsNoTracking`, paginate (keyset for deep pages), add the right indexes, and only for very hot cheap queries consider compiled queries or context pooling. Bypass EF for bulk loading/ETL (`COPY`, SQL scripts), complex reporting SQL (raw SQL via `SqlQuery`/`FromSql` or Dapper on the same connection), or when profiling proves EF overhead dominates a hot path; note licence terms of commercial bulk libraries.
